items.title: Headlines for October 28, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: In Israel, there’s no clear winner so far in Tuesday’s national election. The final tally could take days. It was Israel’s first election since the October 7, 2023, attack and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. With over 70% of the vote counted, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party leads with 27 seats, ahead of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party at 22. Neither candidate is on track to form a governing majority of 61 seats in the Knesset. According to Haaretz, a possible pro-Netanyahu coalition currently has 54 seats, while a possible pro-Eisenkot bloc has 49 seats. Palestinian parties — the Joint List and Ra’am — have won 17 seats, their strongest showing ever. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties. Meanwhile, millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza were ineligible to vote.

Europe is warming at roughly twice the global average. The proposals would bring climate scenarios into decisions on infrastructure and public investment. items.excerpt: At least 68 dead in Spain after one high-speed train slams into another stopped on tracks URDA, Spain (AP) — In central Spain, a high-speed train crashed into another train's rear, killing at least 68 people on Wednesday. Authorities in Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll. The crash injured at least 80 people, and rescue workers are searching for survivors. The accident involved two high-speed trains traveling from Madrid to Seville. The RENFE train hit the IRYO train, causing derailment. Rail service between Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia has been suspended. Emergency workers are focusing on rescuing survivors. This is the second major train accident in Spain this year, raising concerns about rail safety. JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis are closely awaiting final election results and what they mean for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government. Vote counting indicates no clear winner, leading to potential weeks of negotiations to form a coalition for a majority of seats in parliament. Arab-led parties could play a crucial role in coalition-building. Netanyahu remains defiant, dismissing partnerships with Arab parties. His main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, is open to such alliances. Still, the polls indicate Netanyahu's Likud party has lost seats but remains the largest. There is the potential for another election if no government is formed. WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump wants midterm voters to imagine he's on the ballot and has seized the political spotlight in a way that makes such make-believe seem a bit more real. He's making 30-plus campaign stops around the country with low approval ratings, and he organized a pre-midterm convention in Dallas and used taxpayer-funded ads to promote himself. Trump believes injecting himself into races whenever possible is the best way to win. His strategy has sometimes backfired, as during the 2018 midterms. This time, polls suggest more voters disapprove of Trump than support him. Democrats are therefore betting on a backlash, and have spent heavily on advertising focusing on Trump and his administration's policies. KHERSON, Ukraine (AP) — Officials say that a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine has held for its first day and night. The truce began Tuesday and aims to provide food, medicine, and evacuation for about 2,000 residents. If successful, it will be the first significant truce since Russia's invasion over four years ago. U.S. First Lady Melania Trump brokered the humanitarian mission, and Pope Leo XIV urged for aid and safe evacuations. Meanwhile, the war continues elsewhere, with Russian drone strikes in Kharkiv and Ukrainian drones downed in Russia.

items.title: Fed keeps interest rates steady despite rising inflation
items.excerpt: Oct. 28, 2026, 2:01 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 28, 2026, 2:44 PM EDT By Steve Kopack, Maya Huter and Brian Cheung The Federal Reserve on Wednesday voted to keep interest rates unchanged, its final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections. The decision to hold rates steady came despite rising inflation that jumped from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced that the central bank will reduce the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates from eight to seven next year and by two in 2028. Warsh said that the seismic change to the schedule would help improve the “quality” of its decisions. A major driver of that inflation is the soaring cost of gas, diesel and crude oil. These higher prices have hit consumers hard, and many economists say the spillover effect of rising gas prices has started to show up across the broader economy. In its post-decision statement, the Fed acknowledged the problem that inflation is causing but said it needs more data before moving forward with a rate hike. “Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, PCE, will not be released until Thursday, but it is expected to touch 3.7%. “This suggests that the Fed might not be done tightening and future hikes will depend on the incoming data,” said economists at Morgan Stanley. In central bank speak, tightening refers to raising rates. “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” said chairman Warsh in a post-meeting press conference. “That’s good news, but inflation is too high.” “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” he added. Wednesday’s vote was not unanimous, unlike September’s 12 to 0 vote to hike rates, the first time since 2023 that the central bank had raised its benchmark rate. Two officials, governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a rate hike. The dissent by Cook, whom President Donald Trump is attempting to fire, was her first ever.

items.title: Fed holds rates steady as it awaits ’accumulation of more information’ By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Oct 28, 2026, 02:03 PM Updated Oct 28, 2026, 03:00 PM WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation. In a 10-2 decision, the US central bank said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated," upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal," the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. "The Committee will deliver price stability." Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision, favoring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favor of the same rate increase. The Fed’s latest policy statement is a notable change from the September 15-16 meeting, with a hint of the sort of forward guidance Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to avoid. The central bank’s assessment of the economy was upgraded to "strong" from the "solid" expansion seen as of the September meeting, while investment was still described as robust and job gains were viewed as keeping pace with the workforce. Market reaction was muted, with US stocks paring gains slightly after the decision. US Treasury yields extended their rise, with the 10-year Treasury note yield at 5.028%. Short-term interest-rate futures rose a bit, as traders pulled back a bit on bets of Fed rate hikes ahead. "A hold isn’t relief," said Kelly Brown, the CEO of deposit management company Ampersand. "It’s the Fed telling Main Street to wait. With inflation still at 3.7%, and oil above $100 a barrel, businesses can’t count on borrowing costs coming down anytime soon." FEARS THAT INFLATION IS BROADENING The outcome of this week’s meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy. Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries. ... Investors continue to expect further rate hikes will be needed, beginning in December and continuing into 2027, to lower inflation that is currently around a percentage point above the Fed’s target and has shown little progress in recent months. The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control.

items.title: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections ...
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability. The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month. The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target.

items.excerpt: - AP - Oct 28, 2026 - Oct 28, 2026 Updated 22 mins ago Ken Burns wins a $250,000 prize for bringing American history to life NEW YORK (AP) — Ken Burns has won a $250,000 prize for his contributions to American history. The New York Historical awarded him the inaugural David M. Rubenstein Prize for the Advancement of American History. The jury praised Burns for his work on topics like the American Revolution and the Civil War. They noted his films have brought the history of the U.S. to more people than perhaps any other single body of work. Burns expressed gratitude, acknowledging the collective effort of historians and archivists. The award was established earlier this year by financier David M. Rubenstein. California appeals court upholds actor Danny Masterson's rape convictions LOS ANGELES (AP) — A California appeals court has upheld actor Danny Masterson’s convictions and long prison sentence for raping two women at his home in 2003. The three-judge panel on Tuesday unanimously found that the “That ’70s Show” actor had failed to demonstrate that the lower court made errors that would warrant granting him a new trial. Masterson was convicted in 2023 of raping two women at his home two decades earlier. He was sentenced to 30 years to life in prison. His attorneys said in an emailed statement Tuesday that they would seek review at the California Supreme Court. Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at his rape and sex assault trial LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand says allegations of sexual misconduct have had a “devastating” impact on his life. The actor and comedian testified in court Wednesday at his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault. Brand, 51, denied all charges, stating that friends and colleagues have abandoned him. He also mentioned being barred from staying with his baby son in the hospital due to the allegations. Over the past two weeks, prosecutors have presented their case, with six women accusing Brand of misconduct between 1999 and 2009. Brand insists that consent is fundamental, denying any wrongdoing. Iran sentences acclaimed film director Jafar Panahi to new prison term after his return home CAIRO (AP) — Iran has sentenced acclaimed film director Jafar Panahi to five years and one month in prison, following his return to the country earlier this year, after the start of U.S. and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic. The Tehran court also ordered the confiscation of Panahi’s “movable and immovable assets.” That's according to his lawyer Mostafa Nili, who spoke in an interview with the reformist news site Emtedad on Tuesday. Nili did not say what Panahi was convicted of. But the director, who returned to Iran in March, had been previously convicted of “propaganda activities against the system.” Susan Saint James, Emmy-winning actor of 'McMillan & Wife' and 'Kate & Allie,' dies at 80 LOS ANGELES (AP) — Susan Saint James, known for her roles in “McMillan & Wife” and “Kate & Allie,” has died at 80. People magazine reports she passed away Monday after a battle with pancreatic cancer. Born in Los Angeles, she started modeling in Paris as a teenager and later signed with Universal Studios. She gained fame in the 1970s and 1980s, earning multiple Emmy nominations. Saint James retired to focus on family but occasionally appeared on TV. She was a longtime supporter of the Special Olympics and leaves behind her husband, children, and extended family. Taylor Swift, Lyle Lovett and more inducted into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Taylor Swift has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, alongside Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Bruce Channel and J.I. Allison. Swift signed her first publishing deal in Nashville at the age of 14. She returned to the city on Monday during the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame annual gala celebration. She said it was an incredible honor to be inducted and described soaking up the lessons from other writers like a sponge. Also honored was country music icon George Strait with the organization's Career Maker Award. He said the songwriters helped to make his career. Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The NFL, Apple Music, and Roc Nation announced the news Monday night. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he always wanted Jay-Z to perform when the time felt right. Jay-Z expressed excitement about the opportunity, calling it a dream come true. His Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to produce entertainment presentations, including the halftime show. Jay-Z, who has won 25 Grammy Awards, will perform at the stadium where he recently celebrated the 30th anniversary of his debut album, “Reasonable Doubt.” Andrea Bocelli concerts in Indonesia to proceed despite opposition from Muslim clerics JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli's concerts in Indonesia will proceed despite opposition from the country's top Muslim clerical body. The Indonesian Ulema Council demanded the cancellation due to Bocelli's past support for Israel. Indonesia, a strong supporter of Palestinians, does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. The concerts are scheduled for October 31 at Borobudur Temple and November 3 in Jakarta. Promoter Shoemaker Live insists the events will support Indonesia's tourism and culture sectors. Bocelli plans to dedicate songs to humanity and world peace. The council argues the concerts could hurt Indonesians who support Palestinians. After pushback, the Dutch reverse course and withdraw from Eurovision again AMSTERDAM (AP) — The Netherlands is withdrawing from participating in the Eurovision Song Contest, reversing a decision in September to return to the show. NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country announced in September it would send a performer to the event, after a subsidiary had said a month earlier it would boycott the contest for a second year. Earlier this month, hundreds of NPO employees sent a letter opposing Dutch participation. A number of prominent Dutch media personalities also publicly objected to the move.
